The word "sound" as a noun has three distinct meanings in English. By far the most important — the one you will encounter in almost every context — is the first one below.

A sound is anything you hear. The bark of a dog, a clap of thunder, the note from a piano, a baby's cry, the hum of a refrigerator — all of these are sounds. If your ears can detect it, it is a sound.

How Sound Is Created

A sound doesn't simply exist on its own. It always begins with something vibrating — moving back and forth very rapidly. Here is how the process works:

Imagine you pluck a guitar string. The string vibrates, moving back and forth perhaps hundreds of times each second. As it does, it pushes the air molecules directly around it. Those molecules push the ones next to them, and so on — creating a wave of pressure that travels outward in all directions, much like the ripples that spread across a pond when you drop a stone into it.

When this wave of pressure reaches your ear, it makes your eardrum vibrate in a matching pattern. Your brain receives these signals and turns them into the experience of hearing: a sound.

One critical point: sound needs matter to travel through. It moves through air, water, wood, metal, and other substances. But in a vacuum — a completely empty space with nothing in it — sound simply cannot travel. This is why space is utterly silent.

The Four Properties of Sound

Every sound has four qualities that define what it is like:

1. Pitch — How High or Low
Pitch is what makes a mouse's squeak sound different from a lion's roar. A squeak is high-pitched; a roar is low-pitched. Pitch is determined by how fast the vibration is. Fast vibrations produce high-pitched sounds; slow vibrations produce low-pitched sounds. The measurement unit for this speed is the Hertz (Hz), which counts vibrations per second.

2. Loudness — How Soft or Powerful
Loudness (also called volume) is simply the strength of the sound. A whisper is a very soft sound. A thunderclap is extremely loud. Loudness depends on how much energy goes into the vibration — the stronger the push, the louder the sound. Loudness is measured in decibels (dB).

3. Tone (or Timbre) — Its Unique Character
Imagine a violin and a flute playing the exact same musical note at the same loudness. They still sound completely different from each other. That distinctive quality — what makes a violin "sound like a violin" — is called its tone or timbre. It is determined by the mix of additional vibrations (called overtones or harmonics) that accompany the main one. Every voice, every instrument, and every object has its own tone.

4. Duration — How Long It Lasts
Some sounds are instantaneous — the click of a light switch, a hand clap. Others last for seconds or minutes — a held singing note, the drone of an airplane overhead. Duration is simply the length of time a sound continues.

The Range of Human Hearing

Human ears cannot hear all sounds. We are limited to a range roughly between 20 vibrations per second at the low end and 20,000 vibrations per second at the high end. Sounds below this range are called infrasound — elephants, whales, and some other animals use these to communicate across vast distances, but we cannot hear them without instruments. Sounds above this range are called ultrasound — bats use ultrasound to navigate in the dark, and doctors use it to create medical scans inside the body.

No Sound: Silence

The complete absence of sound is called silence. In practice, true complete silence is rare — there is almost always some vibration in the environment. But we use "silence" to describe a state of very little or no audible sound.

How We Describe Sounds

English has a rich vocabulary for describing sounds:

  • Sharp / harsh — sudden, cutting, or grating to the ear (the shriek of a siren)
  • Soft / gentle — low in volume and pleasant (a lullaby)
  • Muffled — when a sound is absorbed or blocked and becomes dull (a voice heard through a wall)
  • Faint / distant — barely audible, as if far away
  • Clear / crisp — easy to hear, without distortion
  • Dull / flat — lacking sharpness or resonance
  • Piercing / shrill — very high-pitched and unpleasant
  • Deep / booming — very low-pitched and powerful (a bass drum)

Echo and Reverberation

When a sound wave reaches a hard surface, it can bounce back toward you. If the surface is far away and the bounced sound reaches you as a distinct, separate repetition, that is an echo. If you are inside a room or hall and the bounced sound blends with the original, creating a lingering, full-bodied quality, that is reverberation (or simply "reverb"). Churches and concert halls are often designed deliberately to have pleasing reverberation.

Common Phrases and Expressions

  • "without a sound" — silently, making no noise: "She slipped out of the room without a sound."
  • "not a sound" — describing complete silence: "At midnight, there was not a sound in the house."
  • "a sound of" — referring to a specific noise: "I heard a sound of breaking glass."
  • "to the sound of" — meaning accompanied by a particular noise: "They marched to the sound of drums."
  • "sounds" (plural) — various noises: "Strange sounds came from the attic."
  • "speech sounds" — in linguistics, this is a technical term for the individual units of sound that make up spoken language. For example, the word "cat" is made of three speech sounds: /k/, /æ/, and /t/. Each language has its own distinct set of speech sounds.

In geography, a sound is a large, relatively sheltered body of water. It typically takes one of these forms:

  • A wide inlet of the sea cutting into the land
  • A stretch of water lying between the mainland and a nearby island
  • A passage connecting two larger bodies of water

This meaning appears most often in proper place names. Some well-known examples:

  • Puget Sound — a large inlet of the Pacific Ocean in the state of Washington, USA, on which the city of Seattle sits
  • Long Island Sound — the body of water between Long Island and the Connecticut and New York coastlines
  • Prince William Sound — an inlet in southern Alaska
  • The Sound (Øresund) — the strait between Denmark and Sweden, connecting the North Sea to the Baltic Sea

If you see the word "Sound" as part of a geographical name, it almost always refers to this meaning.

In medicine, a sound is a long, thin, smooth instrument — usually made of metal — that a doctor inserts into a narrow body passage to examine it, measure its depth, or gently widen it. For example, a uterine sound is used in gynecological procedures, and a urethral sound in urology. The instrument is named for the idea of "probing" or "sounding out" a depth, similar to how sailors once used weighted ropes to measure the depth of water. This is a specialized term you will mainly encounter in medical texts.
Meaning 4: A Fish's Swim Bladder (Old, Culinary)

Inside many fish is an organ called the swim bladder — a gas-filled sac that helps the fish control how deep it floats in the water. In older English, particularly in fishing and traditional cooking, this organ is called the sound of the fish. You may encounter references like "cod sounds" in old recipes, referring to this organ prepared as food. This meaning is rare and largely confined to historical texts and traditional cuisine; you are unlikely to come across it in modern everyday use.

MeaningWhat It Is

The noun "sound" most commonly means what you hear — a vibration that travels as a pressure wave through a medium and is perceived by the ear. It has four defining properties: pitch, loudness, tone, and duration. It cannot exist in a vacuum.

As a geographical term, "sound" means a wide inlet of the sea or a water passage between two landmasses — most often seen in place names.

In medicine, "sound" refers to a thin probing instrument used to examine body cavities.

In old English and traditional cooking, "sound" can mean the swim bladder of a fish — a rare and specialized usage.

The first meaning — what you hear — is the one you will use and encounter in the overwhelming majority of situations throughout your life.
